subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Carbon Footprint
description: Learn The Carbon Footprint in one minute.

hook.text: The term 'carbon footprint' was popularized by a BP ad campaign in 2004.

buildup.text: The idea was clever: shift responsibility from corporations to individual consumers.

discovery.text: Your footprint matters, but 100 companies produce over 70% of global emissions.

twist.text: The average American emits 16 tons of CO₂ per year. The global average is just 4.

climax.text: Both personal choices and systemic change matter — it was never one or the other.

punchline.text: Your footprint matters. So does who drew the sidewalk.

details.summary: A carbon footprint measures the total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an individual, product, organization, or activity. The concept was popularized by BP in 2004 to shift responsibility to consumers, but it remains a useful tool for understanding personal and corporate impact.
details.whyItMatters: Carbon footprints help identify the largest sources of emissions in daily life and business operations, even though systemic change matters more than individual action.
takeaways: The average American's footprint is roughly 16 tons of CO2 per year
Flying, driving, and meat consumption are the biggest personal contributors
BP coined the term to deflect blame from fossil fuel companies to individuals

faq.question: What has the biggest impact on a personal carbon footprint?
faq.answer: For most people in wealthy nations, flying, driving a car, and eating meat are the top three contributors. A single transatlantic flight can emit more CO2 per passenger than many people in low-income countries produce in an entire year.

faq.question: Is focusing on personal carbon footprints counterproductive?
faq.answer: Individual action matters but cannot substitute for systemic change. Just 100 fossil fuel companies are linked to over 70 percent of global emissions. Effective climate policy requires both personal awareness and structural transformation.
